title: Checkpoint: Engineering Marvels
objective: After this level you can explain how engineers span rivers, dig tunnels and hold back water.
summary: Galloping Gertie twisted apart in the wind in 1940 because its designers hadn't given that force a path. Every marvel in this chapter finds each force and gives it a way to the ground.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: four months after it opened, a bridge twisted itself apart.
cards.body: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State, nicknamed Galloping Gertie, opened on July 1, 1940. On November 7, 1940, in a wind of about 42 mph, it tore apart. No people died, because the bridge had been closed to traffic in time. What went wrong?

cards.headline: The force nobody gave a path
cards.body: Its deck was narrow, just two lanes, and stiffened by solid plate girders instead of open trusses. Those girders didn't absorb the wind's gusts, and the deck began to twist, each swing larger than the last. The replacement, opened in 1950, used a web truss, and the collapse spurred research into how wind acts on bridges. Later suspension bridges were designed with its lessons.

mascot.line: Every marvel in this chapter is a list of forces, each with a path. Gertie's list was missing one.

cards.headline: Engineering Marvels: every force needs a path

items.label: Across a gap
points: Beams bend, arches push, cables hang (Level 51)
Arch dams push the water into the valley sides (Level 55)

items.label: Rock and water
points: A tunnel is an arch that goes all the way round (Level 54)
Water pushes hardest at depth, so dams thicken at the base (Level 55)

items.label: The ground itself
points: Piles carry loads down to firm ground (Level 58)
Base isolators let the ground move beneath (Level 59)

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Why every great structure must give each force, even the wind, a safe path to the ground.
How beam, arch, suspension and cantilever bridges each carry weight across a gap.
Why dams are thickest at the bottom, and how an arch dam pushes water into the valley sides.
How foundations, retrofits and base isolators keep buildings up on soft or shaking ground.

questions.prompt: What brought down the first Tacoma Narrows Bridge in November 1940?

options.label: An earthquake shaking the ground under its towers
options.rationale: Wind, not an earthquake, destroyed it.

options.label: A ship striking a pier
options.rationale: Nothing hit it; the wind did it.

options.label: Wind of about 42 mph that set its deck twisting
Its cables rusting through
options.rationale: It failed four months after opening, in the wind.

questions.explanation: In a wind of about 42 mph, Galloping Gertie's deck twisted in ever larger swings until it tore apart.

questions.prompt: What was wrong with Galloping Gertie's deck?

options.label: Its narrow deck had solid girders that didn't absorb gusts
It was too heavy for its towers
options.rationale: Weight wasn't the problem; wind was.

options.label: It was built on soft ground, like the tower at Pisa
options.rationale: The failure was in the deck, in the wind.

options.label: It had no cables at all
options.rationale: It was a suspension bridge, hung from cables.

questions.explanation: The narrow two-lane deck had solid plate girders instead of open trusses; they didn't absorb the gusts, so it twisted.

questions.prompt: Engineering Marvels recap: which Chapter 1 shape do both a tunnel's lining and an arch dam borrow?

options.label: The post and lintel
options.rationale: Lintels bend; tunnels and arch dams stay in compression.

options.label: The cantilever
options.rationale: Cantilevers belong to bridges like the Forth.

options.label: The steel frame
options.rationale: Frames hold up buildings, not dams.

questions.explanation: A tunnel is a continuous arch that goes all the way round, and an arch dam's curve passes the water's push into the valley sides.

questions.prompt: Engineering Marvels recap: what kept the East River out of the Brooklyn Bridge's caissons while workers dug?

options.label: Pumps running day and night
options.rationale: Air pressure, not pumping, kept the water out.

options.label: Compressed air pumped into the boxes

questions.explanation: Compressed air pumped into the bottomless boxes kept the water out while workers dug.

questions.prompt: Engineering Marvels recap: what is a cantilever, the Forth Bridge's building block?

options.label: A beam supported at one end only
A tube sunk into a trench

questions.explanation: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end only, like a diving board; the Forth Bridge joins three of them.
